pages.name: Layers of cubes
pages.text: [[Volume]] counts unit cubes, here 1 m cubes called [[cubic metres]]. A 4 m by 3 m base takes 12 in a layer, so 5 layers hold 12 × 5 = 60 m³. Drag the top.

pages.alt: A base 4 metres by 3 metres, ruled into 12 one-metre squares. 5 layers of 12 one-metre cubes are stacked on it, 60 cubic metres. 12 times 5 equals 60 cubic metres. The top can be dragged up or down a layer at a time.

pages.name: A box tank
pages.task: An example box tank is 3 m long and 2 m wide. Drag its top until it holds 9 m³.
pages.why: Its base is 3 × 2 = 6 m², so each 1 m layer holds 6 cubes. 9 m³ is one and a half layers, so the tank is 1.5 m deep, and 6 × 1.5 = 9 m³.

pages.name: A litre
pages.text: A [[litre]] is the space in a 10 cm cube. Ten of them fit along each edge of a 1 m cube, so 1 m³ holds 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 L.

pages.name: cm³ in a m³
pages.task: 1 m is 100 cm. How many cm³ make 1 m³?
pages.why: A 1 m cube is 100 cm each way. One row of 1 cm cubes along the bottom is 100 cm³, a layer is 100 × 100 = 10,000, and 100 layers make 100 × 100 × 100 = 1,000,000 cm³.

pages.name: A round tank
pages.task: An example round tank is 1.2 m across and 2 m tall. How many m³ does it hold?
pages.why: Halve 1.2 m for the radius, 0.6 m. The round base is π × 0.6² = 1.13 m², and it rises 2 m, so π × 0.6² × 2 = 2.26 m³.

pages.name: Mass from density
pages.task: [[Density]] is mass ÷ volume. An example tank holds 3 m³ of an oil of 850 kg per m³. What is the oil's mass?
pages.why: Density is mass ÷ volume, so mass is density × volume. Each m³ of the oil has a mass of 850 kg, so 3 m³ has 850 × 3 = 2,550 kg.
